lesson.sourceStem: The nurse has four assigned patients. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

initial.question_stem: The nurse has four assigned patients. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

options.label: A
options.text: A patient with blood pressure 150/92 mm Hg and no symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: A postoperative patient with new inspiratory stridor

options.label: C
options.text: A stable patient with a stage 2 pressure injury requesting a scheduled dressing change

options.label: D
options.text: A patient with mild nausea after an antiemetic and no other symptoms

initial.key_cue: The postoperative patient has new inspiratory stridor.
initial.why_correct_short: New inspiratory stridor suggests upper-airway narrowing and may indicate an impending airway emergency. It takes priority over the stable findings listed.

rationales.A: The elevated blood pressure needs follow-up, but the scenario describes no acute symptoms or threatened airway.
rationales.C: The dressing change is needed, but routine wound care can wait while the nurse assesses a possible airway emergency.
rationales.D: Mild nausea without other symptoms is less urgent than new stridor.

initial.one_line_fix: Prioritize a new, potentially time-sensitive threat over stable findings; seek immediate help when airway compromise is suspected.

retry.question_stem: Which patient needs immediate nursing assessment?

options.label: A
options.text: A recently extubated patient with new high-pitched inspiratory noise and difficulty breathing

options.label: B
options.text: A stable patient waiting for a routine dressing change

options.label: C
options.text: A patient with unchanged chronic back pain awaiting scheduled medication

options.label: D
options.text: A patient asking about tomorrow’s discharge time

retry.key_cue: The breathing change is new after extubation.
retry.why_correct_short: New stridor with difficulty breathing after extubation can signal upper-airway compromise and requires immediate assessment and escalation.

rationales.B: Routine wound care does not outrank new breathing difficulty.
rationales.C: Unchanged chronic pain needs care, but the new breathing problem is more urgent.
rationales.D: Discharge planning can wait during assessment of a possible airway emergency.

retry.one_line_fix: Assess the whole breathing pattern and its timing; do not wait for a definitive diagnosis before escalating a threatened airway.
